name: Deep Impact impactor
intro: NASA crashed this impactor into comet Tempel 1 on purpose, on 4 July 2005, to blast out material from inside the comet. It was destroyed in the crash. In 2011 another spacecraft came back and spotted the crater it made.
whyLeft: Crashing was its whole job. It flew on its own for its last day and steered itself into the comet at about 37,000 km/h.
repurpose: Nothing is left to repair. Going back to look was its reuse: NASA’s Stardust spacecraft visited Tempel 1 in 2011 and photographed the crater.

hotspots.title: The crater
hotspots.text: When Stardust flew past in 2011, it found the crater: about 150 meters wide, with a small mound in the middle where material fell back in.

hotspots.title: The flash
hotspots.text: The flyby spacecraft watched from a safe distance as the hit made a bright flash and a huge cloud of dust. The dust was as fine as powder, with water ice and carbon-rich material.

photo.alt: A comet nucleus with a bright burst of light and dust spraying from it.
photo.caption: Comet Tempel 1 just after the impactor hit, seen by the Deep Impact flyby spacecraft on 4 July 2005.

hotspots.title: A copper bullet
hotspots.text: The impactor was built with lots of copper, because copper would not confuse the measurements of what the comet is made of.

photo.alt: Engineers in clean-room suits beside a spacecraft with a big copper-coloured disc.
photo.caption: The impactor on Earth before launch. The copper-coloured front plate is the heavy part that smashed into the comet.
photo.licenseEvidence: Commons page licence: “Public domain” (PD NASA); original source: https://images.nasa.gov/details/05pd0114 http://mediaarchive.ksc.nasa.gov/detail.cfm?media.

hotspots.title: Its last pictures
hotspots.text: The impactor’s own camera sent pictures of the comet’s surface until just seconds before the crash, steering itself to the target.

funFact: The crash happened on 4 July 2005, Independence Day in the USA, so some called it the biggest Fourth of July firework ever.
